How can you write an entire article about atheistic positions on abortion without discussing Peter Singer? I will comment in full later, as this topic is interesting and Singer's arguments are essential to understanding why pro life arguments are far less convincing when you remove God from the equation.

EDIT: Now that I have time... here are my views informed by Peter Singer (though not identical, as I don't agree with him 100%)

Basically, the author's arguments all depend on the idea that human life is special. This position is untenable, in my view, in an atheistic world view. Without a creator who bestows special privileges to the human species, there is no rational basis for using the species barrier as an ethically relevant line-in-the-sand. From a naturalistic viewpoint, we are but one insignificant species, residing on one insignificant planet, in one insignificant solar system, in one insignificant galaxy of billions and billions of galaxies. The naturalistic world view is a humiliating affair for human beings who think that their humanity (i.e. their status as Homo sapiens) is ethically relevant. In a naturalistic world-view, one needs to develop some other basis for ethical principles, as our humanity is not defined by some special place in the universe.

A naturalist has to ask himself, "Why does the life of an embryo matter more than the preferences of the woman carrying it?" The pregnant woman is a thinking, feeling, self-aware being. An embryo (or young fetus) doesn't even have the wiring necessary to feel pain or pleasure. It lacks even the most basic tools to perceive its own existence. Why then, ought we care about its interests? Or to put the question more bluntly, how can it even have interests for us to care about in the first place? At least with an infant, it is sensible to assume that it can have the most basic of interests. A baby has the wiring necessary to feel pleasure and pain, and responds predictably to both. Anyone with the ability to empathize can sense that an infant has rights that are worth respecting, even though it isn't fully developed and therefore doesn't deserve the same rights as an adult human being (i.e. it can't vote). But, the average abortion occurs at or before 12 weeks of gestation, when there is no credible evidence that the fetus has any perceptive abilities. It has no experience, and therefore cannot have any interests to consider from an ethical standpoint. It's only value, in a naturalistic view, is the value it has to other humans. Therefore, it makes sense that the persons most affected by its existence (or lack thereof) ought to decide for themselves what is best. In the case of abortion, priority must be given to the pregnant woman because she has the most to gain or lose from the decision. Even the man who impregnated her hasn't really lost anything yet... at least if the abortion occurs before the fetus develops the ability to experience its own existence.

So what of the arguments in the article? The author argues that because a fetus has potential, its life should be preserved. But, where do we draw the line there? Such an argument, taken to the extreme, would be a great argument against contraception or even against refusing sex. And it fails to consider the real concern that forcing unwanted children to be born may actually increase the amount of suffering that exists in the world. It makes far more sense to prevent unwanted children while fostering a society in which wanted children can thrive.

Saw this posted on the topic of abortion a few months ago and it was so good that I had to save it:

There is a concept called body autonomy. Its generally considered a human right. Bodily autonomy means a person has control over who or what uses their body, for what, and for how long. Its why you can’t be forced to donate blood, tissue, or organs. Even if you are dead. Even if you’d save or improve 20 lives. It’s why someone can’t touch you, have sex with you, or use your body in any way without your continuous consent.

A fetus is using someone’s body parts. Therefore under bodily autonomy, it is there by permission, not by right. It needs a persons continuous consent. If they deny and withdraw their consent, the pregnant person has the right to remove them from that moment. A fetus is equal in this regard because if I need someone else’s body parts to live, they can also legally deny me their use.

By saying a fetus has a right to someone’s body parts until it’s born, despite the pregnant person’s wishes, you are doing two things.

  1. Granting a fetus more rights to other people’s bodies than any born person.

  2. Awarding a pregnant person less rights to their body than a corpse.

• But should the punishment for a breach of body autonomy be death? This hinges on the debate of what constitutes life in the first place. If hypothetically fetuses are alive, then punishing them by death for infringing on a lady is verging on m'lady territory.

• The fetus didn't choose to be born; the implications of this again depend on what constitutes life. If someone throws you into someone else's yard, and you get stuck - are you really trespassing? Can the owner just come and shoot you in the face and claim that this is moral? In this analogy, you're not an inanimate object, and so it's clearly wrong to shoot you in the face.

So I find body autonomy to be a red herring, because the fetus did not choose to be born (the mother on the other hand is much more responsible for the fetus' existence than the fetus is; pregnancy is not some unexplained, de-facto state), and everything hinges on whether this is a person or not - and not so much on the basis of legal technicality, but on the reality of consciousness.

The real question is: are we killing someone? All other questions and implications are contingent on this.
